newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: U.S. First Lady calls for empowerment of women.
newsitem.headline: U.S. First Lady calls for empowerment of women.

text.p: U.S. First Lady Hillary Clinton made a strong pitch for the empowerment of women on Sunday, saying that despite enormous strides "women still find their voices silenced" in too many parts of the world.

In a speech to women of the Philippines, she spoke against selling girls to brothels, child labour, rape and physical abuse, unequal pay practices and not allowing women to participate in government, among other practices.

"In country after country -- from the most advanced democracies to those newly emerging, from the most dynamic free market economies to those reeling from the pace of global change -- women are still striving to define and attain their rightful place in government, the economy and civil society and claim their share of...power," Clinton said.
"...despite the enormous strides we have made, (women) still find their voices silenced and their potential stymied in too many parts of the world," she added.
Clinton was in Manila with her husband, U.S. President Bill Clinton, for the annual summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum on Monday.

She said that since an international women's conference in Beijing last year issued a "call to action" for nations to recognise their progress and prosperity depends on women, many countries have responded positively.

Tanzania, India and Argentina have taken steps to increase the number of women at high levels of government while recent elections in Bangladesh, Japan, Mongolia and Australia have seen an increasing number of women run for -- and win -- political offices, she said.
In Panama reform of the family code has given women more say in alimony, in Namibia women are now afforded equal rights with men in marriage and Thailand passed a new anti-prostitution law, she said.
Further, Egypt has banned female genital mutilation in government health facilities and South Africa is moving to ensure free health care for pregnant women and children under six, she said.
She hailed the Philippines in particular for setting up centres to assist women and children hurt in domestic conflicts and for addressing the sensitive issue of family planning.

President Fidel Ramos and the government deserve praise for an urgent campaign to end the illegal recruitment of Filipinas for overseas jobs through which the rights of women and girls are routinely violated in other countries, she added.
But more must be done across the world.

"Because there is no balance of power in our lives or in our world as long as poverty wears a woman's face...as long as women...are barred from the ballot box...(and) denied equal pay for equal work," she said.
